stories.headline: Justice Department to send election monitors to Adams County for Nov. 3 election
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice notified the Colorado Secretary of State on Wednesday that it will send election monitors to Adams County on Election Day. An Oct. 21 letter from Jake Bachand, a trial attorney in the department's Civil Rights Division, said the monitors will check compliance with federal voting rights statutes. These include the Voting Rights Act, the National Voter Registration Act, the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, the Help America Vote Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act. A similar notice sent to Douglas County was later described by the department as an error.

Bachand wrote that the monitors will only observe, will not interfere in voting and will not talk to voters inside polling places. They will dress in business casual clothing and will not be identified as DOJ personnel by uniforms or pins. Adams County sits in the heart of one of the nation's battleground congressional districts.

Secretary of State Jena Griswold said her office is considering the request with the Attorney General's Office. She wrote that Colorado is not subject to any relevant court orders or settlement agreements, and that the cited statutes do not give the department authority to observe in non-public election spaces. Her office is treating the letter as a request for official observer status under state law, which requires an authorizing letter surrendered to the county clerk or a designee.

stories.headline: Mandatory evacuations, closures in Pagosa Springs area as flooding hits southwest Colorado
stories.summary:
Heavy rain in southwest Colorado prompted mandatory evacuation orders Thursday for low-lying and flood-prone areas along the San Juan, Rio Blanco, Navajo and Piedra rivers. The Archuleta County Sheriff's Office and the Town of Pagosa Springs announced the orders as river levels rose and flooding was expected. Residents were urged to stay away from riverbanks, avoid driving through flooded areas and keep pets away from rising water.

Pagosa Springs closed Town Park, Mary Fisher Park, Centennial Park, River Center Park and Cotton Hole Park. Hiking and biking trails along the San Juan River were closed, as were the boat ramps at San Juan River Park and Yamaguchi Park. U.S. Highway 151 closed south of the U.S. 160 junction between mile points 28 and 33, with no estimated reopening time.

As temperatures fall, precipitation is expected to turn to snow, with potentially more than 10 inches in parts of the San Juans. Updates are expected on the Facebook pages of the Town of Pagosa Springs and the Archuleta County Sheriff's Office, and residents can sign up for the community notification system.

stories.headline: Denver to begin enforcing sidewalk riding and parking rules for Veo scooters Nov. 1
stories.summary:
Denver announced Thursday that it will begin enforcing scooter and e-bike violations involving Veo electric vehicles, citing sidewalk riding and improper parking. A City Attorney's Office review found that Veo was not complying with certain provisions of its city contract and applicable ordinances. Enforcement begins Nov. 1, and residents will be able to report Veo-related concerns directly to city officials.

Mayor Mike Johnston said riders should ride and park responsibly and that the city expects Veo to help reinforce those expectations. Councilmember Chris Hinds, who sponsored the ordinance and requested the contract review, helped develop the enforcement effort. He said a change that took effect July 1 puts responsibility on the operator and gives it technology to comply.

Hinds said Veo's own numbers showed more than 338,000 sidewalk-riding events in its first two months, calling it a compliance problem. City staff have met with Veo several times, prompting the company to announce plans to issue fines for sidewalk riding, add parking corrals and improve sidewalk-detection technology. The city says it will keep working with Veo until the issues are resolved.

stories.headline: RTD to offer free bus service on key Boulder routes during Sundance Film Festival
stories.summary:
The Regional Transportation District will offer zero-fare service on key Boulder-area routes and expand schedules during the Sundance Film Festival, which runs Jan. 21 to Jan. 31. The festival, which moved to Boulder from Park City, Utah, is expected to draw 40,000 to 50,000 visitors to a region where January is typically slow. RTD General Manager and CEO Debra Johnson said the plan is meant to reduce congestion and improve venue access.

RTD will add late-night and early-morning rides and a temporary line, Route CHAT, to reach events at Chautauqua Park. The Flatiron Flyer between Denver and Boulder will run until 2 a.m., and SkyRide routes AB and AL to Denver International Airport will add buses. Those routes will charge regular fares.

Operating costs for the free portion will come from Clean Transit Enterprise grant funds and $1 million approved by the RTD Board for a high-volume event service pilot designed to add capacity for Broncos games. Past Sundance editions generated an estimated $13.8 million in Utah state and local tax revenue annually, according to a 2024 Sundance Institute report.

stories.headline: New areas of DIA's Great Hall open as $2.1 billion project nears completion
stories.summary:
Denver International Airport has opened several spaces in the Jeppesen Terminal that had been under construction as part of the Great Hall project. The new areas include a meet-and-greet space for international arrivals and a new North Security Checkpoint, according to an airport news release.

The renovation carries a cost of $2.1 billion and is progressing toward a 2027 completion. The openings mark a milestone for a project that has reshaped the terminal for several years.

The new security lanes and passenger areas are intended to improve the experience for travelers at one of the nation's busiest airports.

stories.headline: Colorado gains authority to permit underground carbon dioxide injection wells
stories.summary:
Colorado now has the authority to permit Class VI carbon capture and sequestration facilities, rather than relying on the federal Environmental Protection Agency's permitting program. The state joins six others with that authority: Arizona, Texas, Louisiana, West Virginia, Wyoming and North Dakota.

Class VI wells are used to inject carbon dioxide deep underground for long-term storage. State primacy means Colorado regulators, rather than the EPA, will review and approve such projects within its borders.

The change is significant for the state's energy and climate policy, as developers weigh carbon capture projects and regulators decide how they will be overseen.

stories.headline: Tour bus driver dies in crash after singer Sawyer Hill's Denver show
stories.summary:
A tour bus carrying singer Sawyer Hill and his band ran off the road and flipped near the Colorado-Wyoming border in the middle of the night on Oct. 14, killing the driver. Hill had performed at Denver's Bluebird Theatre on Oct. 13 and was headed to a show in Salt Lake City. Several band and crew members were injured.

The New York Post reported the driver, identified as David Jackson, 50, a father of four, suffered a medical emergency that caused the bus to cross three lanes of traffic before rolling. Hill said the cause remains under investigation.

Hill has postponed all remaining North American dates of his Everybody's Home, Nobody's Happy tour. Denver was the 14th of a planned 30 shows in the United States and Canada. Tickets remain valid for rescheduled dates, and refunds are available at point of purchase.

stories.headline: Denver7 interviews Democratic gubernatorial nominee Phil Weiser
stories.summary:
With less than two weeks until the election, Denver7 interviewed Democratic nominee and Attorney General Phil Weiser, who is running for governor. The conversation covered topics ranging from water issues to the state budget.

Weiser cited his handling of the opioid crisis as an example of his problem-solving record, saying the state recovered close to a billion dollars from pharmaceutical companies and has seen more than a 20% decline in opioid overdoses. He said the attorney general's office offers a deep view of state agencies and issues.

Weiser criticized his Republican opponent, Victor Marx, for not taking part in debates or unscripted appearances. He said Marx received questions in advance at their one joint appearance, and that he has taken part in forums in Colorado Springs, Grand Junction and elsewhere without advance questions. Election Day is Nov. 3.

stories.headline: Colorado home sales drop 15% in September as buyers gain leverage
stories.summary:
Statewide closed home sales fell 15% in September from a year earlier, the Colorado Association of Realtors reported. Pending contracts slid 11%, and closed sales in the seven-county Denver metro sank 19%. The statewide median price slipped 1.6% to $540,000, and Denver's eased 1.7% to $565,000.

Active listings statewide shrank 2.7% to 34,824. In the Denver metro, nearly 49% of September sales involved a price cut and about 64% came with seller concessions; 80% had at least one. Homes with a price cut sat a median of 68 days, while those without one sold in nine. Townhome and condo medians fell 7% to $395,000.

Realtors said mortgage rates climbed from roughly 6.9% to 7.6% during September, according to Mortgage News Daily data, and that most September closings began before that jump. Some markets bucked the trend: Evergreen and Conifer posted a 36% jump in single-family contracts, while Durango and La Plata County hold nearly eight months of supply.

stories.headline: Thunder beat Nuggets 96-84 in season opener
stories.summary:
The Oklahoma City Thunder beat the Denver Nuggets 96-84 in their home opener Thursday. Jalen Williams scored 21 points, and Chet Holmgren had 12 points and 17 rebounds. The Thunder withstood a poor shooting night from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, whose streak of 20-point games ended at 141 regular-season games.

The Nuggets started Trevon Brazile in place of Aaron Gordon, who was held out for rest. Denver opened the 2026-27 season after a first-round playoff exit last season, the first time since 2022 it failed to win a series.

The Nuggets open their home schedule Saturday against New Orleans.

stories.headline: DeMar DeRozan and the Nuggets look to find fit as veteran sixth man
stories.summary:
DeMar DeRozan arrived in Denver this summer as a super-sub for a team seeking bench scoring. The Nuggets signed the 37-year-old, a six-time All-Star and the 18th-leading scorer in league history, to a one-year veteran minimum contract in August.

Denver has lost depth in four consecutive offseasons, most recently Peyton Watson via sign-and-trade and Tim Hardaway Jr. in free agency. Last season the team failed to win a playoff series for the first time since 2022.

Former teammates Rudy Gay and Amir Johnson described DeRozan as a beloved, stoic teammate with a sly sense of humor, and the Nuggets value his reputation in the locker room.

topStory.headline: Rep. Ilhan Omar Says She Will Leave Washington Home After Federal Agents Search It in Immigration Fraud Probe
topStory.summary:
Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, said Wednesday that she will move out of her Washington, D.C., home after federal agents searched it last week. In her first interview since the Oct. 12 search, given to MS NOW host Chris Hayes, she said the publicity has made her address public and left her family unsafe, citing death threats. "I can't continue to live there," Omar said, adding that she did not want her children visiting while people tracked them.

Omar said 15 to 25 Homeland Security Investigations agents surrounded the residence around 6 a.m. and pounded on the door while she, her husband and her 20-year-old son were inside. She said agents broke the front door as she dressed to answer it, then executed a search warrant that lasted four to five hours. They seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children's book and a vintage camera that was a gift to her husband. Omar described the agents as "intrusive but polite," saying they logged what they took and returned everything else to its place. She also said she believed the early hour was meant to rattle her.

According to a person briefed on the matter who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity, federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives. The Justice Department has said only that it is a criminal investigation. Omar, who was born in Somalia, came to the U.S. with her family at age 12 after they obtained asylum and became a naturalized citizen in 2000. She said she is "confident in the fact that I didn't do anything wrong," and she denied allegations of immigration fraud, remarking that it would be a leap to indict a 12-year-old for conspiring to defraud immigration services.

The search follows a long-running feud between Omar and President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly criticized her character, faith and Somali heritage. On Tuesday, Trump called her a "sick, very dishonest person who hates our country." Asked whether she could face deportation over alleged misstatements in her immigration paperwork, he said, "Well, she could be. She could also go to jail." Allies of the president, including cabinet officials and right-wing influencers, have promoted unsubstantiated claims that she married her brother, which Omar says originated on a Somali blog before being picked up by conspiracy theorists in Minneapolis. She said she believes the raid was meant to appease Trump loyalists.

The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who questioned its timing less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections that will determine control of the House and Senate. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative steps involving candidates shortly before an election. Omar is seeking reelection in a heavily Democratic district centered on Minneapolis and is expected to keep her seat. The investigation is ongoing, and no charges have been announced.
